text: OneLake is included with every Fabric tenant, and Microsoft's own framing is genuinely deliberate: think OneDrive for data. There's exactly one OneLake per tenant — you can't create a second one, and there's no infrastructure to provision. Every workspace, every Lakehouse, every Warehouse in your tenant stores its data inside this single, shared lake.

Here's the claim that genuinely changes how you design pipelines once you internalize it. Every Fabric workload — Data Factory, Spark notebooks, T-SQL queries, Power BI reports — reads and writes the same physical data in OneLake. A Dataflow Gen2 loads into a Lakehouse table; a data scientist attaches a Spark notebook directly to that same table with no connector and no export, because it's already sitting there as Delta Parquet, an open format Spark reads natively.

The other half of one copy of data is the shortcut — a reference to data stored somewhere else, made to look and behave as if it were stored locally in OneLake. A shortcut can point at another workspace, another OneLake item, or an entirely external source. Instead of building a Copy activity purely to duplicate a table into your own workspace, create a shortcut instead — the source updates, and your shortcut reflects it immediately, with no scheduled refresh pipeline required at all.

That's what makes one copy, many engines technically possible in the first place: OneLake stores tables in genuinely open, standard formats, not something proprietary locked to a single engine. Any tool that speaks Delta Parquet can read OneLake data directly, without Microsoft needing to build a custom connector for every possible consumer.

When a Dataflow Gen2's destination is set to Lakehouse Tables, you're not just picking a storage location — you're writing directly into OneLake, instantly available to every other workload in that workspace.
